title: Cloud Communications Platform Guide: How to Choose the Right Communication Platform
description: How to evaluate cloud communications platforms across calling, messaging, meetings, contact-center workflows, integrations, security, network readiness, and total cost.
author: Emily Nakamura

sections.title: Identify the communication use cases
sections.body: List the communication jobs the platform must handle: internal meetings, business phone numbers, customer support queues, call recording, team messaging, webinars, or external contact-center operations. These are related but not interchangeable capabilities. Estimate users, locations, concurrent calls, peak meeting attendance, international calling needs, and any shared-device or frontline-worker requirements. A clear workload map prevents a low-cost meeting tool from being selected for a phone system it was not designed to replace.

sections.title: Test call and meeting quality
sections.body: Assess quality from the offices, home networks, mobile devices, and headsets employees actually use. Run test calls during busy hours and inspect echo, delay, packet loss, jitter, reconnect behavior, and switching between Wi-Fi and cellular data. Confirm supported operating systems, browser limitations, emergency calling behavior, number porting, and local availability before committing. For meeting-heavy teams, test screen sharing, captions, recording, guest access, and large-meeting controls with realistic participants.

sections.title: Review routing and customer workflows
sections.body: If the platform will handle customer calls, test auto-attendants, business-hours rules, queues, voicemail, transfers, call disposition, and escalation to a human. Check whether supervisors can see queue health and whether agents can use the system without switching constantly between tools. For messaging and meetings, test guest policies, retention, search, moderation, and how conversations are connected to projects or customer records. Verify the specific integrations and data fields your team needs.

sections.title: Check security, privacy, and compliance
sections.body: Confirm encryption in transit and at rest, administrative roles, multifactor authentication, single sign-on availability, audit logs, retention settings, and recording controls for the plan under consideration. Call recording and transcription may trigger consent, employment, or data-protection obligations depending on where participants are located. Establish who can access recordings, how long they are retained, and how deletion requests are handled. Ask the vendor for current documentation relevant to your requirements rather than relying on a general compliance badge.

sections.title: Estimate full cost and resilience
sections.body: Compare licenses alongside phone numbers, domestic and international minutes, toll-free service, recording storage, contact-center features, hardware, support, and usage-based charges. Confirm whether the quoted plan includes the features required for your workflows. Ask about status reporting, service-level commitments, regional resilience, data export, and the process for porting numbers away. Model the cost for a normal month and a peak month so unexpected usage does not decide the budget.

sections.title: Run a controlled pilot
sections.body: Pilot with a representative group from IT, customer-facing teams, and remote workers. Include number porting or test numbers, real integrations, mobile devices, accessibility needs, and a fallback contact method. Measure call completion, dropped sessions, support tickets, adoption, and the time needed to complete common tasks. Train administrators and end users separately, document emergency procedures, and expand only after the pilot's acceptance criteria are met.

sections.title: Plan number porting and change management
sections.body: Create an inventory of every business number, its current carrier, its owner, the teams that depend on it, and the call flow that must remain available. Confirm porting requirements and timelines with the receiving provider before cancelling the old service. Communicate changes to staff and customers, update directories and printed materials, and test inbound and outbound calling after each cutover. Keep an agreed fallback route until the business owner confirms that critical numbers and queues work as expected.

sections.title: Define pilot success metrics
sections.body: Before the pilot starts, agree on a small set of measurable outcomes: call completion, dropped-call rate, time to connect, meeting join success, ticket volume, user task completion, and support response. Collect a baseline from the current system where possible and test during representative busy periods. Ask participants to report device and network conditions when quality fails. Use the results to decide whether to adjust network configuration, training, licensing, or provider choice instead of relying only on general satisfaction.
